Q: Query to delete records based on a subquery A:

If you want to delete users where any of the records for that user has tonetone as a meta_value, you can do this:

CREATE TABLE wp_usermeta_users_to_delete
( user_id BIGINT(20) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY );
INSERT INTO wp_usermeta_users_to_delete
SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM wp_usermeta
WHERE meta_value = "tonetone";
DELETE A. FROM wp_usermeta A INNER JOIN wp_usermeta_users_to_delete B USING (user_id);
DROP TABLE wp_usermeta_users_to_delete;*

Q: How can I return a const char * from a C/C++ function? A:

Another way to do this is with unions which works for fixed size strings or character containers. Basically, you reserve a specific memory size as unsigned integer of desired size, and share that memory with another type.

union arduino_signal
{
     uint32_t memory; // or whatever size or type you require
     uint8_t bytes[sizeof(uint32_t)];
};

In Arduino it seems that is possible, but with great care. The thing is that computers know no type, that is human construction. So basically it is similar to uint8_t *bytes = (uint8_t*)ui32_value; with sizeof(ui32_value) being the size of array pointer bytes is pointing to. In C++ there are static and dynamic casting, but this is mostly C remnant. It is still usable, requires a bit of careful handling, but many people tend to go for c++ implementations due what it does under the hood.

From there returning const char * is simply recasting the pointer that points to another value. Or in this case operator const char*() const {return (char*)this->bytes;}.

Keep in mind few things though:

  1. Endianess: Printing won’t print \0 (0) bytes in regular programs due to it being terminator character. So if your machine is big or little-endian it can display 'ASP\0' as 'ASP' or nothing.
  2. uint8_t versus char you can use either or both as they are synonyms. char is 1 byte size, and uint8_t (or any variant) is 1 byte sized. But if you don't use char you will have to cast it into it as shown before.
  3. For larger strings (above 8 bytes) you will have to make additional linked list object (or use existing) to store all that information. This is where strings be buggy comes into play. Unions have fixed size and therefore you can store up to 8 bytes without much effort with clever structures and unions (structures/classes are blocking their data next to each other in memory), so strings rely on heap to fix that which means that data isn't sequential, but wherever. Some compilers optimize that for short strings, some don’t ... so it’s up to you.
  4. If you have large enough data that needs to be read as char arrays I would suggest serialization instead. Heap fracture is not a big deal if you have a GB of memory and cleaning functions as OS, but for Arduino it’s a large chunk of memory that is now corrupted. So if you have to pass textual file over Arduino you don't need Arduino, but something stronger.

Q: Different notation of returning inline struct in C23 A:

However, I could equally write this way (i.e. omit anonymous struct)

Yes and no. It depends on what you mean by "equally". Both signatures are valid, but they are not equivalent, because their return types are not compatible types:

two complete structure, union, or enumerated types declared with the same tag are compatible if members satisfy the following requirements:

  • there shall be a one-to-one correspondence between their members such that each pair of corresponding members are declared with compatible types

[...]

For determining type compatibility, anonymous structures and unions are considered a regular member of the containing structure or union type

(C23 6.2.7/1)

Scalar types such as long are incompatible with every structure type, so the two struct Ret types are not compatible.

Then what's the difference?

The difference is that the two functions have different, incompatible return types. Those two types can serve most of the same purposes, and the syntax for accessing their n member is the same, but they are not interchangeable. Not even if they happen to have the same representation (which is not guaranteed). You need to choose one and stick with it wherever you need compatible types.

Q: How can I create a custom filetype? A:

There are basically two types of storing data:

  1. Binary - you store any information as bytes, here each file type is unique and rigid and can represent a single functionality.
  2. Textual - you write any information in text type, here each file type is versatile and can represent whatever you wish.

A bit of clarity though, how we use data in file isn't its 'functionality' per se. In this term how and what data we write limit how we can 'use' that file, so having a point cloud (bunch of points) can be used to show vector fields, specific shape and so on. But point cloud can’t be used to define a recipe for a solid chocolate cake.

Binary files can be executed, or even appended to executable. What you compile is binary file after all, and as such we call operation of making binary files serialisation or marshaling depending how they are used. Common types are sound files (wav, mp3, ...), image files (png, jpg, ...) and executables (exe, object files, dll, ...).

Textual files can't be executed (without major hacking) and can hold any type of data or content that can be represented textually. Major difference here is encoding and decoding since languages, extended symbols and such can majorly change if your file malfunctions. You read these files one symbol per time and if one symbol is one or more bytes can make a huuuge difference. Common types are comma separated values (csv), html, css, json, ...

A major influence here is combining two, since that is a hard thing to do. Textual files are read symbol by symbol, and as such being able to distinguish between binary and random text can be quite difficult. This is mostly circumvented by beginning and end tags, so you search for textual tags and know that anything between them is binary. But here are some information.

File Type Memory Size Complexity Human readable Computer Readable
Binary (executable) Very Small Extreme No Yes
Binary (storage) Small Medium to High Requires reinterpretation Requires reinterpretation
Textual File Very Large Very Low Yes No

In general, all files should consist of three parts to improve checking and reading, each file is read from the start, so these parts are often used to verify the file as one reads them.

  1. Header - Often containing type of the file (!docstring, <xml, MZ, PNG, EFI, ...), date and time of its creation, version, compression type, table of content... Basically anything that will help you to read/write a file
  2. Body - Content of the file, basically defined by the header.
  3. Footer - Final check if something went wrong.

Textual files can just be bodies (like csv or json files) if their manipulation is straight forward. Binary files though, they have to have these elements.

Use of the files can differ, and basically they either hold data, control a program, keep track or are the program.

Files that hold data are most basic and tend to have least memory strain. They are your data bases, images, sounds, textures, collection of physics and so on. My own recommendation if you can use existing file format, use it. Unless you are inventing something new, there isn't any really need to store data any differently than what already exists. File handlers, manipulators, etc. can already be downloaded or copied from GitHub and that is much less work. Only exception for this is if you want to learn how to build them yourself, but that won’t be usable, but it will be educational.

Files that control a program can control it by changing its functionality (for example, config files) maintain specific cases or are used by another program to build some other program. In C++ terms this would be linker and your cpp, hpp files that tell compiler how to link instructions. My own recommendation if you can use xml, config or ini files go for it. You can link any binary as path to a file to be red, and have other program deal with it.

Files that keep track are different than files that hold data since you can load previous version from existing file, but you can't backtrack from ledger or record. These files are often used for logging, error handling or stuff like that. They most often forgo the header/footer of the file and contain fields as date and time, who, what and where. My recommendation is to toss a coin. Depending on what you need and how, following the standard is highly appreciated for others to understand what it tracks. But it is heavily project dependent.

Files that are the program are most complex, since they tend to hold elements of all other three types. They have data block that define what is used, control a program to define different functionality and uses, keep track what program is executing and finally assembly code that computer understands. My recommendation is to not attempt is unless you really have to, and even if you have to try to find solutions from above 3. Designing these things means that you can design each previous type and understand each intricacies of BIOS, kernel and OS.

So just in case you want to design your own file type, you have to approach this from the middle out.

  1. You decide what it holds that gives you your body of the file type. If your file needs to hold data, is it one type, multiple types... if you file needs to control the program is it controlling setup (is read before program runs, and written after it finishes) or functionality (how program behaves - read during runtime). If your file needs to keep track what is it keeping track of, when its written and read, is it appended ...
  2. From this you get basic information about size of your body, complexity of data for which you are designing your file type. You may want to partition your body into different chunks, are those chunks always the same size or variable?
  3. Now main question is: Can I rely on myself to write a simple program to read/write this? Do I need to know before hand what is content of the file before i read/write it? - Basically its answering the questions of who uses data, what is in data, why is in data, when is made/used and how to use it. Then you trim answers who don't matter (as much) and decide how much of your file type will be human readable.
  4. Ok, now you have body and header. You probably even wrote basic read/write program to use the file. But now, how can you know that you didn't mistype something? Perhaps cosmic ray shined on your computer and inverted few bits? So you find spots in your header and body that require to be true for file type to work and find a way to verify them via hash functions or any other way.

That’s it. You have designed your own file type.

If you come to a point that you feel that you have multiple files in a single file, you are overthinking it or should make multiple individual file types.

On the other hand, you can build file types onto another. For example, let’s make a creature:

  1. What should it hold? Some genetic information, health value, energy value, perhaps some unique moves.
  2. Who uses data? Only creature that data corresponds to. Each data is unique to creature.
  3. Why is it in data? To be able to generate and keep track of the creature status - thus control a file and keep track
  4. When is it made/used? It’s made once two creatures make a new creature, and then that creature is using it every time it runs.
  5. How is it used? It is used mostly when creature performs any action so it should be checked anytime program is called.

So firstly, we know we need some values of limited range of health and energy. We can probably make a 16-bit integer structure that holds that and count each bit as health point, and just build a few methods to simulate reducing and increasing the value of the 16-bit integer.

struct tracker{
    uint16_t data = 0;
    void take(uint8_t how_much);
    void give(uint8_t how_much);
}; // And some printing to display

Secondly, we should code up moves and actions creature can take which we will have to hard code into its own object:

struct creature{
    tracker HP; // Health
    tracker EP; // Energy

    void super_duper_fly(); // Some action
    void court_fancy_pants(); // Making new creatures
    void eat_pizza(uint8_t pizza_value); // Replenishing HP
    void rest();  // Replenishing EP
    void smack_a_bish(); // Fight

}; // And some printing to display

Now we can influence how much Energy or Health creature starts with or gains/loses with each action with some genetic data which let’s say is a genome of 'G'-'A'-'T'-'C' or four bytes - and lets say we have already coded how genes influence all that stuff.

So now we have 2 x 2 byte trackers, four bytes of genetic info so basically we need 8 bytes of body to define all that. We don’t care about time when its made, we don’t care how big it is (always 8 bytes) so we can make due with 8 bytes of body. Reading and writing is straight forward so we are done with body. We just need to tell any program how to recognise it, so we will add 'CREATURE' in Unicode to mark its beginning and another 8 bytes to define checksum for the entire file. That’s it, and we can hold a single creature data.

'C' 'R' 'E' 'A' 'T' 'U' 'R' 'E' // Header 8 bytes
 HP  HP  EP  EP 'C' 'T' 'A' 'G' // Body: creature info 8 bytes
 FF  FF  FF  FF  FF  FF  FF FF  // Footer: check sum 8 bytes

Is it a good file? Nahh... but it’s an example. So now we just say that once creature_x.exe is called it first check if it has this file appended to end of it, if it doesn't it generates random four bytes for genes and implements Health and Energy. If it has, it then can perform any action. If momma and poppa creatures make a baby, they copy their entire binary (without creature part) and mix their genes then appending it to their child. And there we go, we have made a creature executable that is independent with appendix of our own custom file.

So what’s my point of this whole example? Applications of your files are endless, you can have files that change themselves, files that control how they are changed, etc. For most cases, file type is already defined somewhere you just have to look it up. In specific cases (as this example) you might need to make your own, but keep it simple and stupid. It is easier to make file types if you already have entire system defined, rather than making a file type for project on go. So designing files is mostly part of refactoring rather than coding.

Q: This version of CLI is only compatible with Angular versions ^15.0.0, but Angular version 16.0.0 was found instead A:

It is erroring because you have Angular 16 installed but the CLI is version 15.x.

To upgrade Angular CLI, you can use the ng update command. For example, to update to the latest stable release of the core framework and CLI, you can run:

ng update @angular/cli @angular/core

You do not have to use the latest version, but the CLI must be at or above the version of Angular you wish to use.

https://angular.io/cli/update

I would recommend (and I advise this for all Angular upgrades, especially if you use Angular material), that you use the exceptionally excellent interactive upgrade guide.

This link for example will show you all the steps for your version gap.

https://update.angular.io/?v=8.2-15.0

The command you show in your example is from 16 to 15 which would be a downgrade, the tool won't support migration in that direction. You can only go from a lower version to higher version.
